name: Noni fruit extract

lead: Noni is a tropical fruit spread across the Pacific by Polynesian sailors, used traditionally as a tonic and now sold as juice, supplements and in cosmetics. People use it as an antioxidant for a brighter, more youthful complexion.

The chain is antioxidant: the fruit contains anthraquinones, iridoids, flavonoids and scopoletin, and an anthraquinone from noni was reported to boost extracellular matrix synthesis in cultured human skin fibroblasts. That is cell-culture work; Wikipedia states there is no confirmed clinical efficacy for any use, and no skin-appearance trial was identified.

paras: Taken as a juice or supplement, or applied in creams and serums, usually as part of a wider anti-aging routine. Users describe gradual changes over weeks.

Anthraquinones can be harmful, and a 2024 review is cited as linking oral noni products to liver disease risk. The FDA issued a 2018 warning letter to a noni marketer over unapproved drug claims. People with liver conditions commonly avoid oral noni.

angle.text: Noni extract is sold as juice, supplements and cosmetics as an antioxidant for a brighter, more youthful complexion. An anthraquinone from the fruit boosted extracellular matrix synthesis in cultured skin cells, which is the route to firmer-looking skin.

lead: Noni fruit extract comes from Morinda citrifolia, a tropical shrub of the coffee family (Rubiaceae) that Polynesian sailors carried across the Pacific. The pungent fruit was eaten as a famine food, and its leaves, bark and roots were used in traditional medicine and as dyes.[1] Today it is sold as juice, powders, capsules and as an ingredient in lotions, soaps and seed oils.[1]

In appearance care, noni is positioned as an antioxidant botanical for skin and hair. Its pitch rests on constituents such as anthraquinones, iridoids, flavonoids and scopoletin.[1] Laboratory work has reported that an anthraquinone from the fruit induced extracellular matrix synthesis in cultured human skin fibroblasts, the kind of activity associated with firmer-looking skin,[2] and a formulation study paired noni with pandan leaf extract in an anti-dandruff shampoo.[3]

Wikipedia states there is no confirmed evidence of clinical efficacy for any intended use, and it cites a 2024 review linking noni supplements and drinks to a risk of liver disease through anthraquinone exposure.[1] In July 2018 the US FDA issued a warning letter to a noni marketer over unapproved drug claims.[1] No trial of noni on skin appearance was identified.

paras: Morinda citrifolia is a shrub or small tree reaching about 6 m, with large opposite leaves, white tubular flowers and a multiple fruit that gives off a strong odour when ripe. It flowers and fruits year-round, tolerates saline soils and drought, and was assessed as Least Concern by the IUCN in 2024.[1]

Austronesian voyagers took the plant into the Pacific as a canoe plant, and it is now cultivated across the tropics and widely naturalised.[1] Indigenous communities ate the fruit during famines, which earned it the nickname starvation fruit, and on some islands it was a staple eaten raw or cooked. Southeast Asian and Aboriginal Australian cooks used it with salt or in curries, and leaves appear in Thai and Cambodian dishes.[1] Polynesians reportedly used green fruit, leaves and roots as a general tonic, and bark and roots served as dyes, including by Yolngu artists in Arnhem Land who dye pandanus fibres with it.[1]

Reported constituents include anthraquinones (among them damnacanthal), lignans, polysaccharides, flavonoids, iridoids, scopoletin, catechin, beta-sitosterol, fatty acids and alkaloids. Fruit powder supplies moderate carbohydrate and fibre, while the juice is sparse in nutrients.[1]

A pharmacokinetic study used scopoletin as a marker of noni exposure and noted the lack of product standardisation across the many noni products sold worldwide.[4] Food-technology work has examined stabilising noni extract by microencapsulation with gum arabic and maltodextrin for powders.[5]

sections.h: Use in skin and hair care
paras: Consumer noni products include lotions, soaps and seed oil.[1] Cosmetic positioning generally leans on antioxidant and skin-conditioning claims. A 2005 laboratory study reported that an anthraquinone isolated from noni fruit induced extracellular matrix synthesis in normal human fibroblasts,[2] and a 2021 formulation study combined noni and pandan leaf extracts as a candidate anti-dandruff shampoo.[3]

In bodybuilding forums, noni appeared mainly as an oral supplement. A 2001 T Nation thread asked about Morinda citrifolia and the alkaloid xeronin in the context of recovery, and a 2006 thread discussed noni juice opinions, with posters pointing to Wikipedia's description of promotion of the juice as a cure for various conditions.[6][7] These are individual forum posts rather than a body of practice.

Preclinical and food-science studies have examined noni extract for other purposes: laxative activity and low organ toxicity in mice,[8] glucose and lipid metabolism in diabetic mice,[9] memory impairment in mice,[10] antibacterial activity against Listeria as a produce wash,[11] and effects in livestock and shrimp feed.[12][13] A periodontal study evaluated noni extract as a bone regenerative material for intrabony defects using clinical and cone-beam CT assessment.[14] These studies address health or agricultural endpoints rather than skin appearance.
Wikipedia notes that anthraquinones can be harmful and cites a 2024 review in Medicine (Baltimore) reporting a risk of liver disease from noni supplements, beverages, powders, oils and leaves.[1]

On 18 July 2018 the FDA issued a warning letter to Hawaiian Organic Noni, LLC for marketing unapproved drugs and making health claims under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.[1] Published pharmacokinetic work has stated that noni products lack standardisation and that no optimal dose or dosing interval has been established.[4]

No trials of noni on skin or appearance were found. A phase I study of noni in 51 advanced cancer patients sought a maximum tolerated dose using quality-of-life measures; the maximum tolerated dose was reported as 12 g daily in capsules, with no dose-limiting toxicity found and withdrawals at the next level attributed to the difficulty of swallowing so many capsules.[15] A phase I pharmacokinetic study gave freeze-dried fruit capsules to nine healthy volunteers and found that scopoletin entered plasma rapidly, with low bioavailability and considerable variation between people.[4]

A randomized, double-blind, crossover, placebo-controlled study in 30 healthy subjects found that 1 g of noni extract altered alcohol absorption timing and lowered blood acetaldehyde compared with placebo.[16] A registered study of an iridoid-enriched beverage examined skin autofluorescence as a marker of oxidative stress (NCT01597076, n=34),[17] and a phase II prostate cancer trial was terminated after six participants.[18] A phase I study in cancer patients began in 2001 (NCT00033878).[19]
